title: The Farm, the Rabbit, and the City That Was Never Built: Walt Disney from Marceline to Reedy Creek
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Farm, the Route, and the Ambulance

stops.name: Tripp Avenue, Chicago: the fourth son
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date and city from d23.com/about-walt-disney/; the address 1249 North Tripp Avenue, later renumbered 2156 North, and the Hermosa neighborhood from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 2156 North Tripp Avenue, which the gazetteer labels Walt Disney Birthplace House.
stops.campa: Elias Disney has built the house at 1249 North Tripp Avenue with his own hands, in a Chicago district called Hermosa that is still half prairie. Flora, a schoolteacher before she married him, keeps the accounts and the four boys. Their fourth son is born there on the fifth of December and named Walter Elias. The family will not stay long. Elias distrusts cities and distrusts what his older sons are finding in them, and within five years he is reading advertisements for Missouri farmland and asking his brother about the price of an acre near a railroad.
suggested_refs: The Walt Disney Birthplace house at 2156 North Tripp Avenue, Hermosa, Chicago

stops.name: Mojacar, Almeria: the town that claims him
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not fact. Mojacar's own municipal audio guide (mojacar.es/en/audioguias/city-gate-3/, fetched this pass) narrates the story as local lore. No birth record, adoption paper, or genetic evidence supports it; the Chicago birth is documented. Dated to the birth only so the stop sits beside the claim it contests. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of Mojacar, Almeria.
stops.campa: On a hill above the Almerian coast, Mojacar tells a different birth. In the town's own audio guide the boy is Jose Guirao Zamora, son of a washerwoman named Isabel Zamora and a local physician, sent to Chicago and adopted there. No birth certificate exists for Walt in Chicago, the guide says, nor for Jose in Spain, though records survive for his brothers; and the CIA, it adds, used the secret for decades to keep him informing. The same guide records Disney's own answer to the story: a confusion, he said, with a Spaniard named Zamora who worked at his studio.
suggested_refs: The Mojacar municipal audio guide, City Gate 3, as the institutional carrier of the Guirao Zamora legend

stops.name: Marceline, Missouri: the farm and the orchard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the move (historicmissourians.shsmo.org/walt-disney/); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The pin is the Marceline depot, now the Walt Disney Hometown Museum; the farmhouse plot itself could not be separately pinned this pass.
stops.campa: Elias buys a farm outside Marceline, a Santa Fe railroad town in northern Missouri, and moves the family onto it. Walt is four. He draws the animals, sells a sketch of a horse to a retired neighbour doctor for a nickel, watches the trains come through the cut, and eats fruit off trees his father planted. He attends Park Elementary School. Marceline is the town he will keep describing for the rest of his life, and the main street he builds in California thirty years later is this one, as a nine-year-old holds it. Five years after the move the farm fails, and the land is auctioned off from the porch.
suggested_refs: The Walt Disney Hometown Museum in the former Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe depot, Marceline
Main Street, U.S.A., Disneyland, built from the Marceline recollection

stops.name: Benton Grammar School, Kansas City: the route before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the move and for the paper route (historicmissourians.shsmo.org/walt-disney/); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 3004 Benton Boulevard, the school's address; the original building no longer stands.
stops.campa: Elias buys a Kansas City Star delivery route and works his sons on it without wages. Walt is nine. He is up at half past four, walking the route in snow before school, sleeping through his lessons at Benton Grammar School afterward, then delivering again in the afternoon. He keeps the route six years. A classmate named Walter Pfeiffer takes him into vaudeville houses and nickelodeons his father would not have permitted, and on Saturdays he pays for classes at the Kansas City Art Institute out of what he can hold back. The school building at 3004 Benton Boulevard is gone.
suggested_refs: The Kansas City Star and Times delivery route worked by Walt and Roy Disney, 1911-1917

stops.name: McKinley High School, Chicago: The Voice and the war
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the return to Chicago and the two schools (historicmissourians.shsmo.org/walt-disney/); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 2040 West Adams Street, the historic McKinley High School site, now Chicago Bulls College Prep.
stops.campa: The family goes back to Chicago when Elias buys into the O-Zell jelly concern. Walt enrols at McKinley High School on West Adams Street, draws cartoons for the school paper The Voice, and rides downtown three evenings a week to the Chicago Academy of Fine Arts, where a newspaper cartoonist teaches the night class. He is sixteen and the war is on. The drawings he sends to The Voice are war drawings: a soldier, a helmet, a caption. Roy has already enlisted in the navy. Walt does not finish the year.
suggested_refs: The Voice, McKinley High School paper, carrying Disney's earliest published cartoons

stops.name: Chicago: the year on the papers altered
stops.date_confidence: attested. Enlistment date, the falsified birth year, and his actual age from waltdisney.org/blog/over-there-walt-disneys-world-war-i-adventure. Coordinates are the corpus canonical Chicago pin, inherited unchanged, rather than a recruiting-office address, which is not documented in the sources reached.
stops.campa: The army will not take a sixteen-year-old and his mother will not sign for one. So he writes 1900 where 1901 belongs, and Flora signs what is put in front of her. On the sixteenth of September 1918 he is accepted into the American Red Cross Ambulance Corps. Then influenza takes him and he lies at home while his company sails without him. The armistice is signed on the eleventh of November while he is still waiting for a berth. He goes anyway, boarding the SS Vaubin a week later, seventeen years old, bound for a war that has already stopped.
suggested_refs: Disney's American Red Cross Ambulance Corps enlistment papers, bearing the altered birth year 1900

stops.name: Neufchateau, Vosges: cartoons on the canvas
stops.date_confidence: arrival in France on 4 December 1918 attested (waltdisney.org/blog/over-there-walt-disneys-world-war-i-adventure). The specific posting at Neufchateau is reconstruction: the dossier gives it, but no source reached this pass confirms the exact base, so the pin carries the Vosges country generally and not a documented billet.
stops.campa: He lands in France in December and spends most of a year driving for the occupation, hauling relief supplies, officers, and beans through the Vosges country. He is seventeen. He paints cartoons along the canvas sides of his ambulance, and he draws caricatures for the other drivers to send home, and he charges them for it. The country is full of soldiers with nothing to do and pay in their pockets. With a Georgia boy in the unit he works a second line of business, doctoring German helmets into sniper trophies for the souvenir trade.
suggested_refs: The cartoon-painted Red Cross ambulance, described in Disney's own later accounts of the French year

segments.name: Kansas City: The Trick of Making Things Move

stops.name: Pesmen-Rubin Art Studio, Kansas City: the desk beside Iwerks
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the studio, and the meeting with Ub Iwerks (waltdisney.org/blog/how-walt-started-in-animation); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The pin is a declared generic downtown Kansas City point: the Pesmen-Rubin address was not established in this pass.
stops.campa: He comes back to Kansas City in the autumn of 1919 wanting newspaper work and does not get it. Roy finds him a place instead at the Pesmen-Rubin Commercial Art Studio, drawing letterheads and farm-equipment catalogues for the Christmas trade. At the next desk sits a Kansan of Dutch descent his own age, Ub Iwerks, a far better draftsman and much slower with people. The Christmas rush ends and both are let go. Within a week they have hung out their own shingle, Iwerks-Disney Commercial Artists, and inside two months Walt has taken a salaried job to keep them both eating.
suggested_refs: The Iwerks-Disney Commercial Artists partnership, Kansas City, winter 1919-1920

stops.name: Kansas City Film Ad Company: the borrowed camera
stops.date_confidence: attested for the employment and the first animation work (waltdisney.org/blog/how-walt-started-in-animation); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The Newman Laugh-O-Grams premiere of 21 March 1921 is attested to the day in the same source and is narrated here rather than given a stop, since the Newman Theater address could not be pinned this pass. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 2449 Charlotte Street.
stops.campa: The Film Ad company on Charlotte Street makes one-minute advertising reels for local theatres out of jointed paper cutouts, photographed a frame at a time. Disney takes the job and Iwerks follows him in. He borrows a camera from his employer and works nights in the family garage, teaching himself from a library copy of E. G. Lutz's Animated Cartoons, which he keeps out past its due date. On the twenty-first of March 1921 the Newman Theater downtown runs his topical shorts as Newman Laugh-O-Grams. He is paid a hundred and fifty dollars, which is what they cost him to make.
stops.quote: The trick of making things move is what got to me.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, quoted in Walt Disney Family Museum blog, 'How Walt Started in Animation', waltdisney.org/blog/how-walt-started-in-animation
suggested_refs: E. G. Lutz, Animated Cartoons: How They Are Made, Their Origin and Development (1920)
The Newman Laugh-O-Grams, premiered at the Newman Theater, 21 March 1921

stops.name: McConahay Building, Kansas City: Laugh-O-Gram Films
stops.date_confidence: attested. Incorporation on 22 May 1922, the McConahay Building at 1127 East 31st Street, and the staff list from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laugh-O-Gram_Studio; the fairy-tale subjects from waltdisney.org/blog/how-walt-started-in-animation. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of the address, labelled Laugh-O-Gram Studio.
stops.campa: He leaves the day job and incorporates Laugh-O-Gram Films on the twenty-second of May with money raised from Kansas City investors, taking the second floor of the McConahay Building at 1127 East 31st Street. The staff is young and often unpaid: Iwerks, Hugh Harman, Rudolf Ising, Friz Freleng, Carman Maxwell. What they make are the tales of the Grimms and Perrault run through a Kansas City lens: Little Red Riding Hood, Puss in Boots, Cinderella, seven minutes each, with motorcars and telephones in them and jokes about the rent.
suggested_refs: The surviving Laugh-O-Gram fairy-tale shorts, 1922-1923
The restored McConahay Building at 1127 East 31st Street, Kansas City

stops.name: Kansas City: the bankruptcy and the coach ticket
stops.date_confidence: attested for the July 1923 bankruptcy (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laugh-O-Gram_Studio) and for the broken promise of $11,100 by the distributor; day within the month unknown and defaulted to 01. The forty dollars he leaves with is attested by d23.com/about-walt-disney/.
stops.campa: The distributor who promised eleven thousand one hundred dollars does not pay. Salaries stop and the staff drifts away. Disney moves into the office, washes once a week at Union Station, and lives on a can of beans a day and the credit a Greek restaurant downstairs extends him. He photographs a live child against animated backgrounds for a reel he calls Alice's Wonderland and cannot finish it in time. Laugh-O-Gram files for bankruptcy in July 1923. He sells the camera to pay for a coach ticket west. Forty dollars are left over, and the unfinished reel goes into the case with him.
suggested_refs: Alice's Wonderland (1923), the unfinished Kansas City reel carried to California

stops.name: Hollywood: arrival with forty dollars
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved: d23.com/about-walt-disney/ says he arrived in Hollywood in August 1923, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney says July 1923. Dated here to August after the company archive, with the conflict recorded. Coordinates are the corpus canonical Hollywood pin, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: He arrives with forty dollars, a cardboard suitcase, and the unfinished Alice reel, intending to direct live-action pictures and not cartoons at all. Every studio in town turns him down; he cannot get past the gate at most of them. Roy is already in Los Angeles, in a veterans' hospital with tuberculosis. Walt is twenty-one. Whether he steps off the train in July or in August is not settled even by the company's own archive, which says August, against the standard reference works, which say July.
suggested_refs: The Storytellers statue, Disney California Adventure, showing the 1923 arrival with the cardboard suitcase

stops.name: Kingswell Avenue, Los Feliz: the uncle's garage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrangement and the capital: $290 pooled and $500 borrowed, and the camera stand in the uncle's garage, per d23.com/about-walt-disney/. The Kingswell Avenue address of Robert Disney's house is widely reported in company histories; coordinates are the OSM geocode of 4406 Kingswell Avenue. Day of month is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: Uncle Robert Disney rents his nephew a room at 4406 Kingswell Avenue and lets him use the garage. Walt builds an animation stand there out of scrap lumber and shoots on a camera bought secondhand. Roy keeps the books from a hospital bed and writes the letters that raise the money. Between them the brothers pool two hundred and ninety dollars, and Uncle Robert, who does not believe in the business, lends them five hundred more. No distributor has yet answered them about the Alice reel he carried out of Kansas City.
suggested_refs: Robert Disney's house and garage at 4406 Kingswell Avenue, Los Feliz

stops.name: Kingswell Avenue: the Winkler contract
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the contract (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney); the company treats 16 October 1923 as its founding. The Kingswell office address is documented in company histories but was not independently re-fetched; coordinates place it on the 4600 block of Kingswell, adjacent to and distinct from the garage pin.
stops.campa: Margaret Winkler, who distributes Felix the Cat out of New York and runs the only such business in the country headed by a woman, answers the Alice reel with a contract. She signs on the sixteenth of October, and the company will treat that date ever afterward as the day it began. The brothers rent the back room of a real estate office further along Kingswell and hire their first inker to fill in celluloid. Lillian Bounds is one of two girls in the ink and paint room, and Walt drives her home because neither of them owns a car.
suggested_refs: The Alice Comedies (1923-1927), the Winkler series that founded the studio
Margaret J. Winkler's distribution contract of 16 October 1923

stops.name: Lewiston, Idaho: the marriage at her brother's house
stops.date_confidence: attested. Date from d23.com/about-walt-disney/; the marriage at Lillian Bounds's brother's house in Lewiston from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney. Coordinates mark the town centre; the brother's address is not documented in the sources reached. Lillian's 1924 hiring is tagged R in the dossier and uncorroborated.
stops.campa: They drive north to Idaho to be married in her brother's house at Lewiston, on the thirteenth of July 1925. Lillian Marie Bounds is an ink-and-paint girl at the studio and has been for about a year. The honeymoon runs up to Mount Rainier and back and he spends most of it in pain from an abscessed tooth. Three years later he will bring a mouse home with the name Mortimer attached to it, and the family telling has always been that Lillian said the name was terrible and gave him Mickey instead.
suggested_refs: Diane Disney Miller's account of her mother naming Mickey Mouse

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue, Silver Lake: the studio with his name on it
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1926 establishment at 2725 Hyperion Avenue and the 1940 demolition (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of the address, now occupied by a supermarket.
stops.campa: The Kingswell back room is outgrown inside three years. In 1926 the brothers put up their own building at 2725 Hyperion Avenue in Silver Lake, low and white on a street of bungalows, and the sign over the door reads Walt Disney Studio. Roy has agreed the name should be his brother's alone; it sells better, and Roy would rather do the arithmetic. Everything the studio becomes known for over the next fourteen years is made on this lot. In 1940 the buildings come down. A supermarket stands on the ground.
suggested_refs: The site of the Walt Disney Studio at 2725 Hyperion Avenue, demolished 1940

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue: Oswald the Lucky Rabbit
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction. Per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_the_Lucky_Rabbit, Poor Papa was the first Oswald produced but was rejected by Universal for poor quality; Trolley Troubles, released 5 September 1927, launched the series. The per-short fee is contested: silentfilm.org/oswald-the-lucky-rabbit-1927-1928/ gives $2,250, the Oswald article gives $500. Both are recorded; neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: Charles Mintz, who has married Margaret Winkler and taken over her business, brings Universal a rabbit. Poor Papa is drawn first and Universal rejects the reel outright: the rabbit is fat, elderly, and sloppily made. The studio draws him young and Trolley Troubles goes out on the fifth of September 1927. Oswald the Lucky Rabbit sells. Twenty-six cartoons follow within a year, and for the first time since Kansas City the brothers are not in debt. What Universal paid them per picture is given as two thousand two hundred and fifty dollars in one account and five hundred in another, and nothing reached here settles which.
suggested_refs: Trolley Troubles (5 September 1927), the first released Oswald cartoon
Poor Papa, produced first and rejected by Universal

stops.name: Manhattan: the rabbit is not his
stops.date_confidence: attested for the February 1928 trip, Universal's ownership of the Oswald copyright, Disney's refusal, and the loss of most of his staff (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_the_Lucky_Rabbit; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney). The dossier's claim that Mintz made the reduced rate contingent on employee status is dropped: no source reached supports it, and the sources describe a demanded twenty per cent budget cut. Day defaulted to 01. The pin is a declared generic midtown Manhattan point; the meeting's address is not documented.
stops.campa: He goes east in February 1928 to ask for more money per picture and is handed the opposite: a twenty per cent cut, take it or leave it. Then he learns the thing he never checked, that Universal and not he owns the copyright in Oswald, and that Mintz has quietly signed away most of his animators behind his back and can make the rabbit without him. Only Iwerks and three others have refused to go. He leaves the meeting owning none of it. From New York he wires Roy that everything is fine.
suggested_refs: The Universal-Mintz contract of 1927 and its copyright clause

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue: a mouse instead of a rabbit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the train-ride account, which is Disney's own 1948 telling (waltdisney.org/blog/birth-mouse), and for Plane Crazy on 15 May 1928 and The Gallopin' Gaucho failing to find a distributor. Diane Disney Miller's counter-account, that Iwerks refined the drawing and Lillian supplied the name, is recorded in the same source and not adjudicated. The stop is pinned at Hyperion rather than on the train, which has no coordinates.
stops.campa: On the ride home he draws a mouse. His own account, twenty years later, is that the animal popped out of his mind onto a drawing pad while the country went by; his daughter's account is that Ub Iwerks made the drawing that mattered and Lillian supplied the name. Iwerks works behind a locked door at Hyperion, turning out seven hundred drawings a day, while the last Oswalds go out the front and Mintz's remaining men are kept from seeing what is on the desk. Plane Crazy is screened silent in May 1928. The Gallopin' Gaucho follows. No distributor will take either.
stops.quote: He popped out of my mind onto a drawing pad 20 years ago on a train ride from Manhattan to Hollywood at a time when the business fortunes of my brother Roy and myself were at lowest ebb, and disaster seemed right around the corner.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, essay 'What Mickey Means to Me' (1948), quoted at waltdisney.org/blog/birth-mouse
suggested_refs: Plane Crazy (15 May 1928) and The Gallopin' Gaucho, the two undistributed Mickey cartoons

stops.name: Colony Theatre, Broadway: Steamboat Willie
stops.date_confidence: attested. Premiere at Universal's Colony Theater on 18 November 1928, later identified as the Broadway Theatre on 53rd Street (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat_Willie; waltdisney.org/blog/birth-mouse). The quote is Disney's own 1933 statement giving Mickey a 1 October 1928 birthday, superseded later by archivist Dave Smith's ruling for the 18 November premiere: the contradiction is his own and stands.
stops.campa: Sound has arrived and the studio bets everything left on it. A first recording session in Los Angeles fails outright because the orchestra cannot hold to the picture; Disney adds a bouncing visual cue on the film and does it again in New York with Carl Edouarde's men. Steamboat Willie opens at the Colony on Broadway on the eighteenth of November 1928, on a bill under a feature nobody remembers, and every whistle and cowbell falls exactly where the drawing does. Disney speaks the mouse himself. The date becomes Mickey's official birthday, over Disney's own earlier answer.
stops.quote: Mickey Mouse will be five years old on Sunday. He was born on October 1, 1928. That was the date on which his first picture was started, so we have allowed him to claim this day as his birthday.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, public statement, 1933, quoted at waltdisney.org/blog/birth-mouse
suggested_refs: Steamboat Willie (1928), which entered the United States public domain on 1 January 2024
The Broadway Theatre, formerly Universal's Colony Theater, Broadway at 53rd Street

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue: three hundred dollars for the tablet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the deal and Disney's own recollection of it (waltdisney.org/blog/selling-mickey-rise-disney-marketing), which places the licence in a hotel lobby and identifies it as the first merchandising deal, predating Kay Kamen. Exact month and day are not given and are defaulted to 01. The Silly Symphonies start date of 1929 is tagged R in the dossier and uncorroborated this pass.
stops.campa: A man catches him in a New York hotel lobby and offers three hundred dollars in cash to put the mouse on the cover of a children's writing tablet. He takes it. Within four years a Kansas City salesman named Kay Kamen is running the licensing from a New York office, and the mouse is on wristwatches, dolls, toothbrushes, and the sides of trucks. The same year the studio starts the Silly Symphonies, a second series with no continuing character in it, so the animators can practise on anything the music suggests.
stops.quote: As usual, Roy and I needed the money, so I took the three hundred.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, quoted in Walt Disney Family Museum blog, 'Selling Mickey: The Rise of Disney Marketing', waltdisney.org/blog/selling-mickey-rise-disney-marketing
suggested_refs: The Ingersoll Mickey Mouse wristwatch and the Kay Kamen licensing operation

stops.name: Havana: the doctor orders him to stop
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1931 breakdown and the recuperative voyage are standard in Disney biography and are carried by the dossier, but no primary source was reached this pass, and the Havana itinerary and its dates are not documented to landmark precision. Month and day unknown and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He is not sleeping. He cries in story meetings and cannot finish what he is saying, and a doctor tells him to stop working altogether. He and Lillian leave Los Angeles late in 1931 and go east and then south by ship, to Washington and then to Cuba. For some weeks he has nothing to do with the studio at all. He comes back having decided three things: to take up golf and polo, to put a gymnasium on the Hyperion lot, and to get out of the distribution contract he has been paying for.
sources: dossier synthesis of biographical accounts, no primary source reached this pass
suggested_refs: The 1931 collapse, described in Disney's own later interviews as a nervous breakdown

stops.name: Balboa: the canal, and one of the few holidays
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Panama leg of the 1931 rest trip is repeated in popular biographies and carried by the dossier; it was not confirmed against a primary source this pass. The month is an ordering device only, placing the canal after the Cuban leg; no dated itinerary was reached.
stops.campa: The same voyage carries them through the Panama Canal at Balboa, the ship lifted through the chambers and set down in another ocean. Disney takes almost no long holidays in these years and will take fewer once the feature is started; the studio is a payroll that does not pause. What survives in the record of this crossing is the itinerary and the fact of the collapse that produced it. What he thought about while the water rose in the lock is not recorded anywhere reached here, and the biographies that repeat the trip do not claim otherwise.
sources: dossier synthesis of biographical accounts, no primary source reached this pass
suggested_refs: The 1931 recuperative voyage: Washington, Cuba, and the Panama Canal

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue: Flowers and Trees in three-strip colour
stops.date_confidence: attested. Release on 30 July 1932, first commercially released film in full three-strip Technicolor, and the win at the Fifth Academy Awards (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowers_and_Trees; historicmissourians.shsmo.org/walt-disney/). The category name is corrected: it was Short Subjects, Cartoons. Best Animated Short Subject is the post-1971 name and would be anachronistic here.
stops.campa: Herbert Kalmus offers three-strip Technicolor and Disney takes an exclusive on it for cartoons, two years in which no competitor can have the process at all. Flowers and Trees is already half finished in black and white; he scraps the footage and starts again in colour. It goes out on the thirtieth of July 1932 and takes the first Academy Award ever given for a cartoon, in a category then called Short Subjects, Cartoons. Roy says the colour costs too much. Every Silly Symphony made after it is made in colour.
suggested_refs: Flowers and Trees (1932), first commercially released three-strip Technicolor film

segments.name: Disney's Folly and the Burbank Lot

stops.name: Carthay Circle Theatre: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
stops.date_confidence: attested. Premiere date and the cost of about $1,499,000 from d23.com/about-walt-disney/; the theatre at 6316 San Vicente Boulevard and its coordinates from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthay_Circle_Theatre. The Griebel garden-gnome consequence is carried from philipp_griebel.journey.json, which cites English Wikipedia for the causal claim, and is not independently verified here.
stops.campa: Snow White takes three years, several hundred artists, a purpose-built multiplane camera, and about one million four hundred and ninety-nine thousand dollars borrowed against the studio and the house; the trade press calls it Disney's Folly and waits. It opens at the Carthay Circle on the twenty-first of December 1937 and the audience stands up at the end. The tale is the Grimms', number fifty-three in their collection, shortened and given the dwarfs their names. In Grafenroda, where Philipp Griebel's workshop has made terracotta garden gnomes since the last century, the trade dates its mass-market boom from this film.
sources: philipp_griebel.journey.json (stop: Disney releases Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs)
suggested_refs: The Grimms' Kinder- und Hausmaerchen no. 53, Sneewittchen
The Griebel gnome workshop at Grafenroda, Thuringia

stops.name: Hyperion Avenue: the letter to Mary V. Ford
stops.date_confidence: attested as a document. The letter of 7 June 1938 to Mary V. Ford, signed by staffer Mary Cleave on behalf of Walt Disney Productions, is reproduced at news.lettersofnote.com/p/women-do-not-do-any-of-the-creative. It is not signed by Disney personally. Pinned at Hyperion rather than Burbank: the Burbank campus was not completed until 1940, so the 1938 letter went out from Hyperion.
stops.campa: A young woman named Mary V. Ford writes to the studio asking how she might be trained as an animator. The reply, dated the seventh of June 1938, comes back over a staff signature on the company's behalf: the creative work is not done by women, and the only department open to girls is the one where the drawings are traced onto celluloid and the colour filled in. It is a policy statement, not an opinion, and it is typed on the studio's own letterhead. The letter survives and is reproduced everywhere eighty years later. What became of Mary V. Ford, whether she drew again or wrote to anyone else, is not recorded in the source that preserves it.
stops.quote: Women do not do any of the creative work in connection with preparing the cartoons for the screen, as that work is performed entirely by young men.
stops.quote_source: Rejection letter dated 7 June 1938 to Mary V. Ford, signed by Mary Cleave for Walt Disney Productions, Ltd., reproduced at news.lettersofnote.com/p/women-do-not-do-any-of-the-creative
suggested_refs: The 1938 Mary V. Ford rejection letter, Letters of Note

stops.name: Buena Vista Street, Burbank: the new lot, Pinocchio and Fantasia
stops.date_confidence: attested for the completed Burbank complex, the staff of over a thousand, and the two 1940 releases (d23.com/about-walt-disney/); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 500 South Buena Vista Street. Two relations are carried in: Maurice Sendak's account of Fantasia deciding his vocation is stated as fact in maurice_sendak.journey.json; Stravinsky's complaint over the Rite of Spring is documented film history but is not stated in igor_stravinsky.journey.json and was not independently sourced this pass.
stops.campa: Snow White's money buys land in Burbank and a campus laid out like a small corporation: air conditioning, animation buildings turned for the north light, a coffee shop, a machine shop, more than a thousand on the payroll by the time it opens in 1940. Pinocchio and Fantasia are both finished here that year and both lose money, because Europe has closed. Fantasia carries a re-edited Rite of Spring that Igor Stravinsky afterwards says he was underpaid for and musically mangled by; it also decides the vocation of a twelve-year-old in Brooklyn named Maurice Sendak, who keeps the fixation for life.
sources: maurice_sendak.journey.json (stop: at twelve he sits through Walt Disney's Fantasia)
suggested_refs: Sendak's Mickey Mouse imagery in In the Night Kitchen (1970)
Stravinsky's published objections to the Fantasia use of Le Sacre du printemps

stops.name: Burbank: Art Babbitt dismissed
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier dated Babbitt's firing to the eve of the walkout; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_animators%27_strike dates it to February 1941, along with sixteen other Screen Cartoonists Guild members, and identifies that termination as the trigger. Day within the month unknown and defaulted to 01. The dossier's description of Babbitt as guild president is unsupported by any source reached and is not used; he was a leading organiser.
stops.campa: Art Babbitt animates the Queen in Snow White and Geppetto in Pinocchio and is paid better than almost anyone on the floor. He also organises for the Screen Cartoonists Guild, and pays the dues of assistants who cannot afford them out of his own salary. In February 1941 Disney dismisses him along with sixteen other Guild members. Disney has told the staff for years that the studio is a family and that talent will be recognised without a contract; the men who worked eighteen-hour days on Snow White and saw none of the profit have stopped believing it.
suggested_refs: The Screen Cartoonists Guild organising drive at Walt Disney Productions, 1940-1941

segments.name: The Picket Line and the Good Neighbour

stops.name: Buena Vista Street, Burbank: the strike
stops.date_confidence: attested with two corrections. The strike ran 29 May to 21 September 1941, three months and twenty-six days (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_animators%27_strike), not the five weeks the dossier and the general Walt Disney article carry; five weeks at most describes the picketing before federal intervention. The dossier's claim that a federal mediator ruled for the guild on every issue is overstated and not used: the NLRB asked Disney to sign, and the U.S. Conciliation Service brokered the terms.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of May the artists walk out. The line runs along Buena Vista Street carrying placards drawn by some of the best draftsmen in America, and Babbitt shouts at Disney through the car window as he drives through it. It lasts from the twenty-ninth of May to the twenty-first of September, not the five weeks the studio's own histories prefer to remember. The National Labor Relations Board asks Disney to sign a union contract and he agrees; federal conciliators in Washington settle reinstatements, pay equalisation, a salary structure, and a grievance procedure.
suggested_refs: The Animation Guild's own institutional history of the 1941 Disney strike

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the Good Neighbour tour
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tour, its government sponsorship, and the films that came out of it (d23.com a-to-z 'South America'; the strike article notes his absence on the Latin American goodwill tour cooled tensions and that the union threatened pickets in South American cities on his itinerary). The month is an ordering device: the sources reached date the trip to 1941 without fixing its start. Saludos Amigos premiered in Rio in August 1942 and reached United States release in February 1943.
stops.campa: The State Department sends him to South America in 1941 with a party of artists and a government guarantee against losses, while the picket line is still up at home. The itinerary covers Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Peru. In Rio he is received as though he were a visiting minister, and the union threatens to picket the cities on his route. The sketchbooks the party fills become Saludos Amigos, which premieres in Rio in August 1942 and does not reach the United States until the following February.
sources: Alphaville Journal, analysis of the 1941 goodwill tour (cited in dossier, not re-fetched)
suggested_refs: Saludos Amigos (1942) and The Three Caballeros (1944)
The Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs and its cultural programme

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the gauchos and the dubbing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Argentina is named among the countries visited on the 1941 goodwill tour in company histories, but the Buenos Aires leg's specific sites and dates were not confirmed to landmark precision this pass. The month is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: In Buenos Aires the party goes out onto the pampa to watch men ride, and Goofy is put into a gaucho's clothes for El Gaucho Goofy. The programme is cultural diplomacy paid for by a government that wants Latin America kept out of the Axis orbit. Its by-product is a Spanish-language Disney that a continent grows up inside, dubbed and retitled and sung in translation, taken for decades as though it had always been theirs. What the party gathers here and in Brazil goes into The Three Caballeros.
sources: dossier account of the goodwill tour, Argentina leg not independently pinned
suggested_refs: El Gaucho Goofy, from the Saludos Amigos anthology
The Spanish-language dubbing tradition of Disney films in Latin America

stops.name: Washington: the friendly witness
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the date. Disney was among the October 1947 friendly witnesses (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_blacklist; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Ten), but neither article gives per-witness dates, and the dossier's 24 October could not be corroborated this pass. The 1947 hearings were held in the caucus room of what was then the Old House Office Building, now Cannon, a matter of congressional record; the exact room was not re-fetched.
stops.campa: He testifies in October 1947 in the caucus room of the Old House Office Building, as a friendly witness, and names Herbert Sorrell of the painters' union and others he holds to have been Communist agitators behind the strike of 1941. He tells the committee the walkout was Communist-led. Nineteen unfriendly witnesses are called in the same weeks; ten of them go to prison for contempt of Congress and the blacklist starts from there. Which day in October Disney sat in that room is not stated in any source reached here.
sources: govinfo.gov, HUAC hearing transcript (cited in dossier, not re-fetched this pass)
suggested_refs: Hearings Regarding the Communist Infiltration of the Motion Picture Industry, 80th Congress, October 1947

segments.name: The Backyard Railroad and the Park

stops.name: Carolwood Drive, Holmby Hills: the Lilly Belle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the address and the naming of the railroad after it (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolwood_Pacific_Railroad). The dossier gives 1949/1953 for land purchase and construction; the year here is an ordering choice within that span, with month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 355 North Carolwood Drive, filed by OSM under Westwood though Holmby Hills is the correct neighbourhood.
stops.campa: He buys land in Holmby Hills, builds the family a house at 355 North Carolwood Drive, and lays half a mile of one-eighth-scale track through the back garden with a live steam locomotive on it, named the Lilly Belle for his wife. The cars are built in the studio machine shop by men on the payroll. The line crosses a trestle and runs through a tunnel driven under Lillian's flowerbed, which she permits only on condition that it go under and not through. Years before anyone calls it a park, the shape is here already: a loop of track with a berm thrown up around it. Guests sign a liability waiver before they are allowed to ride.
suggested_refs: The Carolwood Pacific Railroad barn, preserved at Griffith Park, Los Angeles

stops.name: Burbank: WED Enterprises
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the date. The 1952 founding of WED Enterprises and its later renaming as Walt Disney Imagineering are carried from the dossier chronology and were not corroborated against a company source this pass; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Pinned at the Burbank studio, from whose staff WED was drawn; WED's own premises are not pinned here.
stops.campa: He forms WED Enterprises in 1952, his own company and not the studio's, and staffs it out of the lot with art directors, machinists, and model builders who have never built anything that stands up outdoors. The initials are his. What it exists to design has no precedent in the trade: not a fairground, not a world's fair, not a zoo, and no category on any bank's lending schedule. The organisation outlives him under the name Walt Disney Imagineering, and the word it coins for its own staff passes into English. The park is drawn before anyone has agreed to pay for it.
stops.quote: It takes a lot of money to make these dreams come true.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, quoted in Walt Disney Family Museum blog, 'Selling Mickey: The Rise of Disney Marketing', waltdisney.org/blog/selling-mickey-rise-disney-marketing
sources: dossier chronology entry, uncorroborated this pass
suggested_refs: WED Enterprises, later Walt Disney Imagineering, and its early Disneyland design files

stops.name: Burbank: an hour a week on ABC
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The dossier dates the Disneyland series premiere to 1954 as part of the park's financing arrangement, uncorroborated this pass; the day is an ordering device only. Pinned at the Burbank studio where the programme was produced, since the dossier records the event only as a national broadcast with no place.
stops.campa: No bank will lend against an amusement park, and the two strong networks will not either. ABC, the weakest of the three, will trade: an hour of programming a week in exchange for a share of the park and a guarantee on its loans. The programme is called Disneyland. Each week the host walks the audience through the construction of the thing the programme is named after, with the dirt still moving behind him. It is an hour-long advertisement and the country tunes in to it voluntarily. The ratings put it near the top of the national list.
sources: dossier chronology entry, uncorroborated this pass
suggested_refs: The ABC television series Disneyland (1954- ) and the network's equity stake in the park

stops.name: Anaheim: the park opens
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the location, the $17 million figure, and the live broadcast (d23.com/about-walt-disney/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney). Opening-day details beyond these are traditional and widely repeated rather than sourced here. The dedication quote is tagged R: it is reached only through Wikiquote in this pass, not through a recording or a Disney facsimile of the plaque.
stops.campa: Orange groves in Anaheim, seventeen million dollars, and roughly a year of construction. It opens on the seventeenth of July 1955 to an invitation-only crowd that turns out to be far larger than the invitations issued, in a heat wave, with the asphalt still soft, some drinking fountains dry, and a live television broadcast going wrong on air in front of the country. Walt reads the dedication from the flagpole in the hub. He says afterwards that the place will never be finished, and treats that as an operating instruction rather than a slogan.
stops.quote: Disneyland is your land. Here age relives fond memories of the past, and here youth may savor the challenge and promise of the future.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the Disneyland opening-day dedication, 17 July 1955; reached in this pass only through en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Walt_Disney, not through the original recording or a Disney facsimile of the plaque
suggested_refs: The Disneyland dedication plaque at the flagpole, Town Square
The Partners statue by Blaine Gibson, dedicated at the castle hub 18 November 1993

stops.name: Squaw Valley: the Olympic pageantry
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline. Disney's chairmanship of the pageantry committee for the 1960 Winter Olympics is part of the documented public record of those Games and is carried by the dossier chronology; it was not re-fetched to a primary source this pass. Day of month is an ordering device; the Games opened on 18 February 1960.
stops.campa: The organising committee of the 1960 Winter Olympics hands him the ceremonies. He builds them the way he builds a park opening: massed choirs, releases of doves and balloons, a torch and a flame, entrances timed to the minute. He is chairman of the pageantry committee, working on ground he does not own, for a crowd that has not paid to enter anything of his, and the Games last two weeks and then the valley empties. In the Sierra the snow does not arrive until the last days before the opening.
sources: dossier chronology entry citing the documented public record of the 1960 Winter Olympics, not re-fetched this pass
suggested_refs: The 1960 Squaw Valley Winter Olympics pageantry committee records

stops.name: Hollywood: Mary Poppins and P. L. Travers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the date. The 1964 release is carried by the dossier chronology and is uncorroborated this pass; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The pitch letter to Travers is attested and quoted at waltdisney.org/blog/look-closer-recap-mary-poppins-pl-travers. The pin is the corpus canonical Hollywood pin, inherited unchanged, rather than a premiere venue, which is not documented in the sources reached.
stops.campa: P. L. Travers refuses him for twenty years. His early letter proposes that her stories would be ideal material for a combination of flesh and blood characters with cartoon, which is exactly the thing she does not want anywhere near Mary Poppins. She signs at last with script approval written in, comes to Burbank, and argues over lines, over songs, and over the colour red. The film is released in 1964 and becomes the most decorated thing the studio makes in his lifetime. Travers weeps at the premiere, and not from pleasure.
stops.quote: It is our thought that these stories would be ideal material for a combination of flesh and blood characters with cartoon.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, letter to P. L. Travers proposing the adaptation, quoted at waltdisney.org/blog/look-closer-recap-mary-poppins-pl-travers
sources: dossier chronology entry for the 1964 release, uncorroborated this pass
suggested_refs: The Disney-Travers correspondence held by the Walt Disney Family Museum

segments.name: The Florida Project and the City That Was Never Built

stops.name: Flushing Meadows: four pavilions at the World's Fair
stops.date_confidence: attested that WED built four sponsor-funded pavilions at the 1964-1965 New York World's Fair and that Audio-Animatronics and continuous-loading ride systems were industrialised there. Coordinates are inherited byte-identical from robert_moses.journey.json, which pins the fairground he presided over. The Moses relation is tagged R: the Moses file never names Disney, and the connection rests on his presidency of the fair corporation that contracted the pavilions. Day is the fair's opening date.
stops.campa: Robert Moses, president of the fair corporation and master of the ground at Flushing Meadows, wants Disney in his fair and gets him: four pavilions, every one of them paid for by a sponsor rather than by the studio. Pepsi and UNICEF take a boat ride through singing dolls. General Electric takes a theatre that revolves around its audience. Ford takes a ride in its own convertibles. Illinois takes a mechanical Abraham Lincoln that stands up out of a chair and speaks. Millions ride them, and afterwards all four systems are shipped west to Anaheim.
sources: dossier account of the four WED pavilions at the 1964-1965 fair
robert_moses.journey.json (stops on the 1964 World's Fair presidency)
suggested_refs: Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln, it's a small world, Carousel of Progress, and Ford's Magic Skyway

stops.name: The White House East Room: the Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested. The noon ceremony in the East Room on 14 September 1964 and the presentation by Lyndon Johnson from presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-the-presentation-the-1964-presidential-medal-freedom-awards. Coordinates are the White House, a declared landmark pin rather than one supplied by the sources. The smoking history is tagged R in the dossier and not independently re-fetched.
stops.campa: Lyndon Johnson gives out the Presidential Medal of Freedom at noon on the fourteenth of September 1964, in the East Room, to a list of artists, scientists, and public men read aloud one name at a time. Disney is on the list. Mary Poppins opened two months before this, and two months after it he will stand behind his brother in Orlando while the Florida land is finally admitted to. He is sixty-two. He has smoked heavily for decades, often unfiltered, and coughs through story meetings without stopping to explain it.
suggested_refs: Johnson's remarks at the presentation of the 1964 Presidential Medal of Freedom awards

stops.name: Bay Lake, Florida: the land bought under other names
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction. Per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World, the announcement was made on 15 November 1965 in Orlando by Roy O. Disney with Governor Haydon Burns, and 27,443 acres had been assembled through dummy corporations from April 1964. The dossier's attribution of the disclosure to Walt alone overstates his role at that press conference. Coordinates mark the Bay Lake and Reedy Creek area of the assembled property, not an announcement-day landmark.
stops.campa: Agents buying under invented company names assemble twenty-seven thousand four hundred and forty-three acres of central Florida swamp, scrub, and cattle land from April 1964 onward, at prices that would have tripled the moment anyone guessed who was behind them. The Orlando Sentinel works it out first. On the fifteenth of November 1965 Roy Disney and Governor Haydon Burns announce the project in Orlando, with Walt beside them, and what Walt describes to the room is not a park. It is a city, with residents in it.
suggested_refs: The dummy corporations used in the Florida land assembly, April 1964 onward
The Reedy Creek Improvement District, chartered 1967

stops.name: Burbank: the EPCOT film
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the date, carried from the dossier chronology and uncorroborated this pass, though the film is well documented as his last on-camera appearance. The quoted line is attested only by the single transcript at sites.google.com/site/theoriginalepcot/the-epcot-film-video/transcript; no independent source reproducing it was found this pass. The plan's internal details are from the same transcript.
stops.campa: He films it on a Burbank stage in front of an aerial map and a plan of radial boulevards, in a jacket, with a pointer, coughing between takes. It is the last footage taken of him. The Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow is to hold twenty thousand people who live and work in it, the cars and the trucks running underneath, industry at the hub, greenbelt and schools laid out in rings around that. Nobody in it owns a house, because owners vote and renters can be moved.
stops.quote: Everything in E.P.C.O.T will be dedicated to the happiness of the people who live, work, and play here, and those who come here from around the world to visit our living showcase.
stops.quote_source: Walt Disney, on-camera narration, 1966 EPCOT promotional film, transcript at sites.google.com/site/theoriginalepcot/the-epcot-film-video/transcript
sources: dossier chronology entry for the 27 October 1966 filming
suggested_refs: The 1966 EPCOT film, Disney's last on-camera appearance
Frank Lloyd Wright's Broadacre City as the nearest American precedent for a totally designed community

stops.name: St. Joseph Hospital, Burbank: across the street from the lot
stops.date_confidence: attested for the admission on 30 November 1966 and the death on 15 December 1966 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney), and for the date and the ten days after his sixty-fifth birthday (d23.com/about-walt-disney/). The November lung surgery, the death certificate's acute circulatory collapse, and the ceiling-tile scene are carried from the dossier and biographical tradition and were not independently re-fetched. Coordinates are the OSM geocode of 501 South Buena Vista Street, directly across the street from the studio.
stops.campa: An X-ray taken for an old neck injury shows the left lung. They take the lung out in November. He is back on the lot within days and then in the hospital again, across Buena Vista Street from his own studio, close enough to see it from the window. The story his brother tells afterwards is that he lay on his back and talked the Florida layout through the ceiling tiles, counting the squares off as a grid. He dies there on the fifteenth of December 1966, ten days past his sixty-fifth birthday.
sources: dossier synthesis of biographical accounts for the surgery and the ceiling-tile scene
suggested_refs: Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center, 501 South Buena Vista Street, Burbank

stops.name: Forest Lawn, Glendale: the ashes and the rumour
stops.date_confidence: attested for cremation two days after death and interment at Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Glendale (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Lawn_Memorial_Park,_Glendale). Coordinates corrected to the cemetery's own; two earlier pins in the research pool disagreed with each other and both landed elsewhere. The claim that the marker bears Lillian's name alongside his is unverified. The Magic Kingdom opening of 1 October 1971 is attested; Roy's death later that year is tagged R and uncorroborated.
stops.campa: He is cremated on the seventeenth of December, two days after his death, and the ashes are placed at Forest Lawn in Glendale. There is no public funeral. Within a few years a story is running that he was frozen instead and lies in a chamber under the castle at Anaheim, waiting; no instruction, no payment, and no preservation record has ever been produced for it, and the cremation is documented. Roy takes the Florida project through to the end and opens the Magic Kingdom on the first of October 1971, as scheduled.
suggested_refs: The Walt Disney Family Museum, Presidio of San Francisco, founded by Diane Disney Miller and opened 1 October 2009
